scenes.text: Eyelashes freeze here. Cars are left running for hours. And around five hundred people live here on purpose. Wob has already packed a suitcase.

This is Oymyakon, a village in the Sakha Republic, in the far east of Russia. It is often called the coldest permanently inhabited place on Earth. Most videos about it ask how people survive here. That is a fair question. But it skips a stranger one. Why is there a village here at all? Somebody chose this spot, in the middle of all this. By the end of this video, you will know why. And Wob will decide whether to unpack. Wob's plan is simple. Find the chilliest village anyone has ever heard of, move in, and become famous for being cold. Wob has packed a toothbrush, a scarf, and a paper map. The map is upside down. Wob says it is fine.

So here is the real question. In a place this cold, why would anyone stop here at all? Part of the answer is hiding in the name. Oymyakon is usually explained as meaning water that does not freeze. Linguists argue about the exact roots, and some sources trace the word to the Even language while others point to Sakha. But the story told about this valley is the same. Nearby there were warm springs, water that stayed open through the winter. And if you move reindeer across a frozen landscape, open water is not a curiosity. It is the whole point. Wob, who has spent this entire trip complaining about frozen water bottles, suddenly understands. Water you can actually drink, in the middle of winter, is worth walking a very long way for.

Reindeer herders stopped at the springs to water their animals and rest before long journeys. A stopping place became a regular camp. Over time, the camp grew into a permanent village. So Oymyakon did not appear despite the cold. It appeared because, in the middle of all that cold, there was one thing that refused to freeze. Wob, who has never herded anything in its life, finds this deeply moving. Wob is now looking for the spring. Wob does not find the spring. Wob finds a very surprised reindeer.

So how cold is this cold, exactly? On the sixth of February, nineteen thirty-three, the weather station here recorded about minus sixty-eight degrees Celsius. That is about minus ninety Fahrenheit. Guinness World Records lists it as minus sixty-seven point seven. The World Meteorological Organization lists minus sixty-seven point eight. So even the number itself comes with an argument. Either way, it is the lowest temperature on record for a place where people live all year. Well. Almost. Far to the northwest, the town of Verkhoyansk has its own reading from eighteen ninety-two, of about the same number. Some sources say the two towns share the record. Others treat the Verkhoyansk reading as disputed. Rival towns. A tenth of a degree. More than a century of arguing. Wob finds this very relatable. Wob once argued with a fridge for an hour.

There is a second argument, much closer to home. The weather station behind that famous number is not in Oymyakon itself. It sits in a valley between Oymyakon and a neighbouring village called Tomtor, near Tomtor's airfield. Tomtor would like you to know this. Some sources argue that Tomtor, not Oymyakon, is the real Pole of Cold. Oymyakon, meanwhile, has the official monument. So Wob, who wants to move somewhere truly freezing, now has to choose between the village with the monument and the village with the thermometer. Wob suggests sharing. Nobody is interested. It is very cold outside, and nobody is backing down. Wob tries standing exactly halfway between them. Halfway turns out to be mostly a frozen road.

But why is it so cold here to begin with? Oymyakon is not even inside the Arctic Circle. It sits a few degrees of latitude south of it. The cold is a team effort. First, in winter a huge, stable zone of high pressure called the Siberian High settles over this part of Asia. It brings clear, dry skies, and clear skies let the ground lose its heat straight up into space. Second, there is the valley itself. Cold air is heavy. It slides downhill and pools on the valley floor, like water in a bowl, while the mountains around it keep warmer air out. Researchers measuring this valley have found the mountain slopes above it can be far warmer in winter than the valley floor. So the village sits at the bottom of a giant bowl, full of the heaviest, chilliest air around. Wob would like a smaller bowl. Wob briefly considers climbing out of the bowl. Up on the slopes it is warmer. It is also a mountain. Wob stays in the bowl.

In the Soviet era, the state pushed deep into this region. A weather station was set up. An airfield was built near Tomtor. And the record that made Oymyakon famous came from that station in nineteen thirty-three. In other words, Oymyakon became famous for its cold partly because someone finally put a thermometer there. Thermometers, it turns out, are very good at making places famous. Wob makes a note to pack one.

This was also one of the darkest periods in the region's history. In the nineteen thirties, the Soviet Union built a network of forced labour camps across the Kolyma region, part of the Gulag system, largely to mine gold. Prisoners began building the Kolyma Highway in the early nineteen thirties, and forced labour continued on it into the nineteen fifties. Many of them did not survive. The village's story begins with the springs. But the highway that crosses this region was built by people who had no choice.

So what is daily life like? In January, the average temperature here is around minus forty-six Celsius. In late December the sun is up for only about four and a half hours a day. That leaves very little time to do anything outdoors, which, in this weather, may be for the best. Beneath the surface the ground is permafrost, frozen all year, which makes ordinary water pipes very hard to keep working. Many homes use outdoor toilets. Yes, even in January. Cars are often left running for hours, or warmed with a fire before starting, because a frozen engine may refuse to start at all.

Food comes mostly from animals and the river: meat, and fish that in winter is sold frozen solid and stacked like firewood. Farming in frozen ground is close to impossible. Wob decides to test all of this personally. Wob steps outside. Wob does not technically have eyelashes. They freeze anyway. A few minutes later, Wob is back indoors, holding a cup of tea with both hands, quietly reconsidering several life choices. The tea, meanwhile, is cooling at an alarming speed. Wob drinks it quickly. Wob regrets that too.

Children here are tough, but not unlimited. According to Russian news reports, younger pupils in the district get the day off when it reaches around minus fifty-two. The exact cut-off for each age group depends on who you ask. For comparison, plenty of schools elsewhere close for a light dusting of snow. Wob asks whether Oymyakon has snow days. The answer is yes. They are just extremely specific.

And then, the twist. Oymyakon is not cold all year. Summers are short, but they can be properly warm. For a few weeks, the frozen valley turns green. By late June, daylight lasts more than twenty hours. In July twenty ten, the station recorded thirty-four point six degrees Celsius. That is about ninety-four Fahrenheit. Put the record low and the record high side by side, and the gap is roughly one hundred and two degrees. Very few places on Earth have record highs and lows that far apart. Wob, who packed nothing but fur, is suddenly optimistic again.

So why do people stay now? For many families, this is simply home. Some of the toughest locals are not even human. Yakutian horses live outdoors all year in this region, right through the winter. A genetic study published in twenty fifteen found that they descend from domestic horses brought here only a few centuries ago. They adapted to the cold remarkably fast, with compact bodies and very thick winter coats. Wob, whose only adaptation is a large backpack, is impressed. Wob tries to make friends with one. The horse is unimpressed. The horse has clearly seen tourists before. Not everyone stays, though. Life at the Pole of Cold is a choice that families keep making, or don't, every year.

And the cold itself has become a reason to visit. Every spring, the district hosts a festival called the Pole of Cold, with events in villages including Oymyakon and Tomtor. Its star is Chyskhaan, the Sakha Lord of Cold, who reportedly has his own ice residence. In twenty twenty-five, there was even a marathon here. In the cold. On purpose. A village that grew up around water that wouldn't freeze now welcomes visitors because of everything that does. Visitors come to stand next to the Pole of Cold monument, take a photo, and hurry back indoors. So let's add it all up. People stopped here because of water that would not freeze, in a land where almost everything does. A stopping place became a village. A weather station gave it a famous reading, and that reading gave it a name the whole world knows. The highway that crosses the region carries a much darker history. And today, the families who live here stay for reasons that are easy to understand: home, the school, the herds, the weather station, and, lately, visitors. The cold was never the reason to come. It was the price of staying.

So, would Wob move here? The springs are lovely. The summers are a genuine surprise. And the people of Oymyakon have built a real home in one of the hardest places on the planet. But the winters here are long, dark and brutally cold, and Wob packed for a weekend. The verdict is NOPE. This is a place for people who grew up with it, or who truly, deeply love winter: silence, clear skies, and a summer that feels earned. Wob is unpacking. Slowly. With gloves on. Wob will be following the thermometer from somewhere much warmer. So, be honest. How long would you last out there?
